title: Validation and calibration of quantum hardware through the many-body quantum Mpemba effect
authors: Francesco Campaioli, Marco Avesani, Oren Raz, Roderich Moessner, Gianluca Teza
abstract: We introduce a validation process that harnesses engineered many-body relaxation to control and calibrate quantum hardware. On two independently developed neutral-atom processors, we realize the many-body quantum Mpemba effect in an open system for the first time. Initial-state engineering creates fast and slow relaxation pathways: the fast pathway opens access to unreachable mixed-state physics before hardware noise obscures the target dynamics, whereas the slow pathway amplifies hidden imperfections in preparation and control. Computational-basis measurements directly and independently benchmark dynamical reliability, revealing each processor's actual operating window as a many-body simulator. The processors are thus judged by the very dynamics they are built to reproduce. Complementary responses disentangle control errors and drive an adaptive, time-resolved scheme that supplies hardware developers directly actionable corrections, enhancing faithful reproduction of the target dynamics. These results establish many-body relaxation as a transferable validation and calibration tool for programmable quantum processors.
summary: The paper presents a novel method to validate and calibrate programmable quantum processors using the many-body quantum Mpemba effect. By engineering fast and slow relaxation pathways in neutral-atom systems, the authors create a stringent benchmark that quantifies hardware imperfections directly from system dynamics. This establishes relaxation as a powerful, transferable tool for improving quantum hardware fidelity.
main_problem: To develop a validation and calibration process for quantum hardware that is more accurate and scalable than existing benchmarks.
main_result: The authors establish many-body relaxation, specifically utilizing the quantum Mpemba effect, as a transferable tool to benchmark and calibrate programmable quantum processors.
method: They introduce a preprocessing sequence ($P$) before running a target task ($L$), allowing direct measurement of extremal dynamical modes governing the open system's relaxation dynamics.
model_or_system: The experiments are performed on neutral-atom processors (e.g., QuEra's Aquila and Pasqal's Fresnel) trapping Rubidium atoms, modeled as open many-body systems evolving under a Lindblad master equation.
key_observables: Figure of Merit ($	ext{FoM}$), Bhattacharyya coefficient ($	ext{BC}_2$), relaxation trajectories (fast vs. slow decay rates), and excitation density $n(t)$.
important_parameters: The initial state engineering controls the fast and slow relaxation pathways; performance is benchmarked against theoretical predictions.
main_assumptions: Current validation methods are limited by exponential scaling for full tomography, necessitating reliance on specific dynamical benchmarks like convergence to equilibrium.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the overall validation routine (Initial state $ightarrow$ Preprocessing $ightarrow$ Task execution) and show model-dependent evidence of the quantum Mpemba effect signature across different preprocessing regimes on both hardware platforms.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the concept by detailing the methodology using two independent neutral-atom processors, demonstrating the fast/slow relaxation pathways via the Mpemba effect, quantifying performance with a Figure of Merit, and concluding that this process serves as a general calibration tool.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses hardware characterization in AMO platforms (neutral atoms) by linking fundamental non-equilibrium physics (Mpemba effect) to practical quantum control engineering, providing actionable feedback for device improvement.
